questions.question: Complete the productivity diagram by writing the word or words for box A and box B.
questions.answer: Box A: gross primary productivity (GPP); Box B: respiration (energy lost by the plants as heat).
steps: Photosynthesis feeds into box A, the total energy fixed by the plants, which is gross primary productivity.
Part of this energy is used by the plants in respiration and lost as heat (box B).
The remainder is stored as new biomass: NPP = GPP - respiration.

questions.question: State the meaning of the term ecosystem.
questions.answer: A community of living organisms interacting with each other and with their non-living (abiotic) environment in an area.
steps: An ecosystem is a defined area that includes all the living organisms in it.
These living organisms are the biotic part and form a community.
The abiotic (non-living) factors such as temperature, water and light are also included.
The organisms and factors interact, e.g. through feeding and energy flow, so the whole is one system.

questions.question: Choose the correct units for NPP from options A to D (A kg m-1 yr-1, B kg m-2 yr-2, C kJ m-1 yr-1, D kJ m-2 yr-1).
questions.answer: D: kJ m^-2 yr^-1.
steps: NPP is the energy stored as biomass by plants per unit area per unit time.
Energy is measured in kJ, not kg, so options A and B are wrong.
Per unit area gives m^-2 and per year gives yr^-1.
Option C has m^-1, so the only correct option is D.

questions.question: Total NPP is 11 700 units. Leaves contain 34% and wood 39%. Calculate the NPP in the roots.
questions.answer: 3159 units.
steps: Add the leaf and wood percentages: 34 + 39 = 73%.
The roots receive the remainder: 100 - 73 = 27%.
Multiply the total by 0.27: 11 700 x 0.27 = 3159 units.
This is the energy stored as biomass in the roots.

questions.question: Explain how the distribution and abundance of Chthamalus and Balanus on the rock show that they occupy different niches.
questions.answer: Chthamalus lives high on the shore and Balanus lower down, with little overlap, so they use different parts of the habitat and are different niches; Balanus is more abundant overall.
steps: Chthamalus (small oval barnacles) is found only on the upper shore, near the highest level the seawater reaches.
Balanus (larger rounded barnacles) is found on the middle and lower shore, down to the lowest water level, and is the more abundant species.

They overlap only in a small zone, so each lives in a different part of the habitat and tolerates different conditions, e.g. Chthamalus can survive longer out of water and drying, Balanus is limited by drying out higher up.
Different niches reduce competition between the two species.

questions.question: Comment on the reliability of the conclusions from the study of the surfaces on which larvae settled (graph).
questions.answer: The conclusions are only partly reliable: rock with barnacles clearly has the most settled larvae, but stones and bare rock overlap, and there is no information on sample size, what the error bars show, or a statistical test.
steps: Means: rock with barnacles about 49, bare rock about 29, stones about 20 larvae per unit area.
The error bars for rock with barnacles (about 43 to 55) do not overlap with those of the other two surfaces, so the difference is probably real.
The error bars of stones (about 16 to 24) and bare rock (about 24 to 34) just touch, so it cannot be concluded that bare rock attracts more larvae than stones.
It is not stated what the error bars show (SD or range), how many replicates were used, or whether a statistical test (e.g. t-test) was done, and the data come from one study only.

questions.question: Describe how the study of larval settlement on different surfaces could be carried out in a laboratory.
questions.answer: Offer larvae equal areas of different surfaces in controlled tanks, count the settled larvae, and repeat with replicates and controls.
steps: Collect barnacle larvae from seawater, since they swim before settling.
Prepare tanks with equal volumes of seawater and equal areas of each surface type (e.g. different rock or plastic).
Keep temperature, light, salinity and water flow the same in all tanks so only the surface type varies.
Add the same number of larvae to each tank and leave for a set time.
Count the larvae settled on each surface, repeat the test, and compare mean numbers with a control to check reliability.

questions.question: Which row of the table shows the type of factor that affected the plant species in two of these habitats?
questions.answer: D: biotic factor for both.
steps: Cutting the field regularly is the action of a living organism (human activity), so it is a biotic factor.
Competition with trees for water is competition between living organisms, so it is also a biotic factor.
Only row D has biotic for both.

questions.question: What is the percentage increase in the number of moss species between regularly cut fields and uncut fields? Options A 23.3, B 70.0, C 233.3, D 333.3.
steps: Moss in the regularly cut fields = 0.3 species; in uncut fields = 1.0.
Percentage increase = 0.7 / 0.3 x 100 = 233.3%.

questions.question: Suggest reasons for the difference in the mean number of plant species in regularly cut fields and in uncut fields.
questions.answer: Cutting removes tall dominant plants so light reaches smaller species; in uncut fields dominant plants shade and outcompete others.
steps: Regular cutting removes tall dominant plants and their litter.
This lets light reach smaller plants and seeds in the soil, so more species can germinate and survive.
In uncut fields, tall dominant species grow and shade the smaller plants.
Competition for light, water and minerals reduces the number of species that can survive in uncut fields.

questions.question: Which option describes what P represents on the genome size graph? A maximum on a bar chart, B maximum on a histogram, C mode on a bar chart, D mode on a histogram.
questions.answer: D: the mode genome size on a histogram.
steps: P is the tallest bar, so it is the most frequent genome size, the mode.
The bars touch and the x-axis is a continuous variable (increase in genome size), so this is a histogram, not a bar chart.

questions.question: Calculate the frequency of the genome size missing from the graph for class 2 mosses.
steps: Class 1 mosses: 1 + 4 + 9 + 7 = 21 species.
So class 2 has 30 - 21 = 9 species.
Class 2 bars shown: 1 + 4 + 2 = 7, so the missing frequency is 9 - 7 = 2.

questions.question: The mean genome size of class 1 mosses is 0.449 a.u. and of class 2 mosses is 0.920 a.u. Calculate the ratio of class 1 to class 2.
steps: Write the ratio as 0.449 : 0.920.
Divide both sides by 0.920 so that the class 2 value becomes 1.
Class 1 mosses therefore have a genome size about half that of class 2 mosses.

questions.question: Give the evidence from the graphs that supports the suggestion that the chromosomes in class 2 mosses are found in pairs.
questions.answer: The mean genome size of class 2 mosses (0.920 a.u.) is about twice that of class 1 mosses (0.449 a.u.), so the chromosome number (and DNA) is about doubled, as expected if they are in pairs.
steps: The ratio of class 1 to class 2 genome size is about 0.49 : 1, so class 2 is about 2 times larger.
A doubled amount of DNA fits with class 2 having two sets of chromosomes, which are found in pairs.

questions.question: Which row of the table describes the types of adaptation of polar bears?
questions.answer: D: thick fur coat is anatomical, hunting by sitting on ice is behavioural, and producing metabolic water is physiological.
steps: A thick fur coat is a physical structure, so it is an anatomical adaptation.
Sitting on the ice to wait for seals is something the bear does, so it is behavioural.
Producing metabolic water is a metabolic process, so it is physiological.
Only row D has all three in the correct columns.

questions.question: What is the niche of a polar bear? A produces metabolic water, B the Arctic Circle, C controls the population size of seals, D uses the layer of fat beneath the skin.
questions.answer: C: it controls the population size of seals.
steps: A niche is the role of an organism in its ecosystem, including its habitat, food and interactions.
A and D are adaptations (metabolism and fat store), not roles in the ecosystem.
B is only the habitat (location), which is part of the niche but not the whole niche.
C describes the polar bear as a predator of seals, which is its feeding role and its effect on another population.

questions.question: Suggest why a polar bear needs to rely on its fat store to provide it with water.
questions.answer: Fat is oxidised in respiration to release metabolic water, because the Arctic water (ice and seawater) is frozen or too salty to drink.
steps: Fat (a lipid) is oxidised during aerobic respiration.
This oxidation releases water as a product, called metabolic water.
The polar bear cannot easily get fresh drinking water from frozen ice or salty seawater.
So it uses the water made from its stored fat to stay hydrated.

questions.question: Explain the effect that habitat fragmentation could have on the genetic diversity of polar bears.
questions.answer: Isolated groups have less gene flow and smaller gene pools, so genetic diversity falls and inbreeding becomes more likely.
steps: Fragmentation separates polar bears into small, isolated groups.
Gene flow (movement of alleles between groups through breeding) is reduced.
Small groups have a smaller gene pool, so fewer alleles and less genetic diversity.
Inbreeding and genetic drift become more likely, which reduces the ability to adapt to change.

questions.question: Explain how flies evolve resistance to new chemicals.
questions.answer: A random mutation gives some flies resistance; the chemical kills non-resistant flies, so resistant flies survive, breed and pass on the allele.
steps: Random mutations in the fly population produce some individuals with an allele giving resistance.
When the chemical is applied, flies without the allele are killed.
Resistant flies survive and reproduce, passing the resistance allele to their offspring.
Over many generations the frequency of the resistance allele rises in the population (natural selection).

questions.question: Suggest why resistance to these chemicals evolves so quickly in flies.
questions.answer: Flies have short generation times and produce many offspring, so many generations and mutations occur in a short time.
steps: Flies have a short life cycle, so many generations occur in only a few years.
Each female produces many eggs, giving a large population.
A large population over many generations gives many chances for a resistance mutation to arise.
Selection then acts quickly, so resistance spreads within about 10 years.

questions.question: Determine the effectiveness of painting stripes on cattle in reducing biting flies, using the graph and both tables.
questions.answer: Painting black and white stripes is effective, cutting biting flies by about half, but painting black stripes only is not.
steps: Mean flies on body and legs: unpainted about 128, black and white stripes about 58 (about 55% fewer), black stripes about 111 (about 13% fewer).

The error bars of black and white stripes (about 45 to 68) do not overlap those of unpainted (about 114 to 144), so the reduction is probably significant, but black stripes (about 95 to 132) overlap unpainted, so there is probably no real difference.

Table 1 totals: 1971 flies on unpainted cattle, 941 on black and white (52% fewer) and 1707 on black stripes (13% fewer); black and white stripes cut flies on the body by 65% (231 v 662) but on the legs by only 46% (710 v 1309).

Table 2: cattle with black and white stripes flicked tails less (42 v 54) and stamped less (10 v 16), so they were less troubled by flies, whereas black-striped cattle behaved like unpainted cattle (55 and 16); skin twitching was slightly higher in black and white (8 v 5).
So the white stripes (contrast) seem to be needed; limitations are that only black cattle were used, the numbers of cattle and the length of the trial are not stated, and legs still had many flies.

questions.question: Explain the importance of protecting existing forests first (rule 1).
questions.answer: Mature forests already store large amounts of carbon and support high biodiversity, which new plantings take decades to match.
steps: Existing forests already store large amounts of carbon in their biomass and soils.
Clearing them releases this carbon quickly, whereas new trees take decades to store the same amount.
Mature forests contain established habitats and species that new plantings lack.
Protecting them keeps these carbon stores and habitats intact.

questions.question: Suggest why organisations involved in reforestation should work together with local people (rule 2).
questions.answer: Local people know the land and species and their support, and protecting their livelihoods, helps the project succeed in the long term.
steps: Local people have knowledge of the land, soils, species and seasons.
Their support helps the project avoid conflict and be accepted.
Projects that ignore local needs can lose land use or livelihoods, so people may damage new trees.
Working together helps the forest be protected and managed over the long term.

questions.question: Explain two reasons why previously forested areas should be selected for reforestation instead of other wild areas (rule 3).
questions.answer: The soil already supports trees (nutrients, fungi, seed bank), and using it avoids destroying other wild habitats.
steps: Previously forested soil still has nutrients, humus and mycorrhizal fungi that help young trees grow.
The seed bank in the soil and surviving roots help natural regeneration.
Using land that was already forested avoids damaging other wild habitats that may hold unique species.
This limits the loss of biodiversity elsewhere while restoring a forest ecosystem.

questions.question: Explain why a mixture of native species, including endangered and genetically diverse species, should be introduced (rule 4).
questions.answer: Native species suit local conditions and restore food webs; genetic diversity lets the forest adapt, and endangered species are conserved.
steps: Native species are already adapted to the local climate and soil, so they are more likely to survive.
A mixture restores the original food webs and provides more niches for many animals and plants.
Planting endangered species helps conserve them in their natural habitat.
Genetically diverse populations have more alleles, so some individuals can survive disease or climate change.

questions.question: State the meaning of the term population, as it has been used in this context (the human population of the world).
questions.answer: All the individuals of one species (here humans) living in the same area at the same time that can interbreed.
steps: A population is a group of individuals of one species.
The individuals live in the same area at the same time.
Here it is the human population of the world, all humans living now.
The individuals in a population can interbreed with each other.

questions.question: State the meaning of the term sustainable, as it has been used in this context.
questions.answer: Meeting present food needs without reducing the ability of future generations to meet theirs (resources used no faster than they can be replaced).
steps: Sustainable means using resources in a way that can continue indefinitely.
Resources should be used no faster than they can be replaced.
Environmental damage should be kept low so that the land stays productive.
This allows future generations to meet their own food needs.

questions.question: Explain how food production could contribute to the greenhouse effect.
questions.answer: Food production releases greenhouse gases (methane from livestock, nitrous oxide from fertilisers, CO2 from land clearance) that absorb infrared radiation and trap heat.
steps: Food production releases greenhouse gases such as methane, from livestock and rice fields.
Nitrous oxide is released from nitrogen fertilisers, and CO2 from clearing land and burning fuel.
These gases absorb infrared radiation re-emitted from the Earth's surface.
They re-emit it in all directions, so less heat escapes to space and the atmosphere warms.

questions.question: Land occupies 149 million km2 of Earth's surface; 71% is habitable and some is used for food production. Calculate the area used for food production, in standard form.
steps: Habitable land = 71% of 149 million km^2 = 149 x 0.71 = 105.8 million km^2.
The pie chart shows 50% of habitable land is used for food production.

questions.question: Estimate the effect of food production on the ratio of biodiversity of mammals.
questions.answer: About 94 : 6 (about 16 : 1), related to food production : not related.
steps: The pie chart for biodiversity of mammals is divided into a large dark sector (related to food production) and a small pale sector (not related).
The pale sector is about 21 degrees, which is about 6% of 360 degrees.
So about 94% is related and 6% is not, a ratio of about 94 : 6, or about 16 : 1.

questions.question: Explain how food production could be made more sustainable, using the diagram of land area used per kilogram of food products and own knowledge.
questions.answer: Food production could be made more sustainable by eating less beef and lamb and more plant foods, chicken, fish and eggs, which need far less land, together with other measures such as better yields and less waste.
steps: Beef (326 m^2) and lamb/mutton (370 m^2) need over 25 times more land per kg than chicken (12 m^2) and about 100 times more than most crops such as wheat (4), rice (3) and potatoes (1), so reducing meat from ruminants cuts land use.

Using less land leaves more habitat, reducing deforestation and loss of biodiversity, and keeps forests that store carbon; ruminants also release methane, so fewer cattle and sheep reduce greenhouse gases.
Eating at a lower trophic level is more efficient because only about 10% of energy passes to the next trophic level, so plant crops feed more people per hectare.
Sustainable farming methods: crop rotation or legumes to reduce fertiliser, integrated pest management, higher yielding or GM crop varieties, less food waste, and renewable energy.
Evaluation: some animal products supply protein and vitamins, so a balance with plant proteins such as soybeans is needed, and fish farming should not pollute water.

questions.question: In 2016 the moose were not counted. Describe how the data were used to estimate the number of moose in 2016.
questions.answer: A trend line through the earlier counts was extended (extrapolated) to read off the 2016 value.
steps: Moose were counted in earlier years, giving data points on the graph.
A trend line (line of best fit) is drawn through these points.
Because no count was made in 2016, the line is extended to 2016.
The value read from the line is used as the estimate.

questions.question: Calculate the percentage decrease in the number of moose from 1994 to 2016, using the graph.
questions.answer: About 55% decrease.
steps: Number of moose in 1994 = about 7.6 x 10^3; in 2016 = about 3.4 x 10^3.
Percentage decrease = 4.2 / 7.6 x 100 = 55%.

questions.question: Sketch a graph to show the relationship suggested between global warming and the decrease in the number of moose from 1994 to 2016.
questions.answer: A graph with a downward-sloping line: moose numbers fall as global temperature rises (a negative correlation).
steps: Label the x-axis with global (mean) temperature or year, rising to the right, and the y-axis with number of moose.
Draw a line or curve that starts high on the left and slopes down to the right, showing moose numbers decreasing as temperature rises.
If time is used on the x-axis, show two lines on the same axes: temperature rising and moose number falling.
Add units (degrees C and number of moose x 10^3).

questions.question: Calculate the percentage of moose that have 50 000 or more ticks on their bodies, using the frequency table.
steps: Moose with 50 000 or more ticks = 15 + 9 + 4 + 4 + 3 + 6 = 41.

questions.question: Explain how global warming might affect the life cycle of ticks and result in the decline of moose, using all the information including the tick life-cycle diagram.
questions.answer: Warmer winters mean less snow, so more tick larvae and engorged females survive; more ticks per moose cause blood loss and fur loss, so moose are weakened and die.
steps: Global warming gives shorter, milder winters with less snow cover, so more larvae can climb vegetation and attach to moose in autumn (they cannot if covered in snow).
In early spring more engorged females drop onto ground without snow, so fewer die and more survive to lay eggs in June, so the tick population increases.
Warmer temperatures may lengthen the active season and speed up development, so more ticks feed on each moose; the table shows about 19% of moose already carry 50 000 or more ticks.
Each tick removes 200 to 600 times its body mass in blood, so heavily infested moose lose much blood, become anaemic and weak.
Irritation makes moose scratch on trees and lose large clumps of fur, so they lose insulation, lose heat in winter and use more energy.
Weakened moose are less likely to survive or breed (calf survival falls), so the number of moose declines, as in the graph (from 7.6 to 3.4 x 10^3).

questions.question: Describe three characteristics of pioneer species.
questions.answer: They tolerate harsh conditions, produce many small wind-dispersed seeds, and grow and reproduce quickly.
steps: Pioneer species tolerate harsh conditions such as bare rock, extreme temperature and little water.
They produce large numbers of small seeds that are dispersed widely, often by wind.
They grow and reproduce quickly, giving them a short life cycle.
Some fix nitrogen or tolerate low nutrients, starting soil formation for later species.

questions.question: Explain why succession occurs in stages.
questions.answer: Each stage changes the habitat (soil, shade, moisture), making it suitable for new species that outcompete the previous ones.
steps: Pioneer species change the habitat as they grow, e.g. by adding humus and organic matter to the soil.
This changes conditions such as shade, moisture and nutrient levels.
The new conditions suit different species better than the earlier ones.
These species outcompete and replace the earlier species, so the community changes in stages towards a climax community.

questions.question: Determine the effect of the volcanic eruption on environmental temperature, using the graph.
questions.answer: The eruption caused a temporary fall in temperature of about 0.3 C, lowest (about -0.28 C) about 1 year after the eruption, returning to near 0 by about 3 years.
steps: Before the eruption the temperature change varies between about -0.1 and +0.1 C.
After the eruption (time 0) it falls to a minimum of about -0.28 C at about 1 year, about 0.3 to 0.4 C lower than before.
It then rises again and is back to about 0 C by about 3 years, so the cooling effect lasts only a few years.

questions.question: Explain the results shown in the graph, given that sulfur dioxide and ash particles reduce the light passing through the atmosphere.
questions.answer: Ash and sulfur dioxide (sulfate aerosols) reflect and scatter sunlight, so less light and heat reach the Earth's surface and the temperature falls; as the particles settle out within a few years, temperature recovers.
steps: The ash and sulfur dioxide spread through the atmosphere and reflect or scatter sunlight.
Less solar radiation reaches the Earth's surface, so less heat is absorbed and the environmental temperature falls (minimum about -0.28 C at about 1 year).
Less light also reduces photosynthesis, so less carbon dioxide is removed from the air.
Over about 3 years the particles fall out or are washed out of the atmosphere, so more light reaches the surface and temperature returns to normal.

questions.question: One eruption released 5 x 10^7 metric tons of CO2; anthropogenic activities released 3.5 x 10^10 metric tons in one year. How many eruptions in one year would release as much CO2 as anthropogenic activities?
questions.answer: 700 eruptions.
steps: Anthropogenic CO2 = 3.5 x 10^10 metric tons per year.
One eruption releases 5 x 10^7 metric tons of CO2.
So 700 eruptions per year would be needed.

questions.question: Discuss the possible effects of volcanic eruptions on climate change, using the CO2 graph for 1958 to 2004 and the eruptions in 1963, 1980, 1982 and 1991.
questions.answer: Eruptions cause short cooling but do not change the rise in CO2: the CO2 graph shows no obvious change at 1963, 1980, 1982 or 1991, and the steady rise is due to human activity, so eruptions have little long-term effect on climate change.
steps: The CO2 level rises steadily from about 315 to about 387 a.u. between 1958 and 2004, with no clear dip or rise at the eruption years (1963, 1980, 1982, 1991).
One eruption releases only 5 x 10^7 tons of CO2, whereas human activity releases 3.5 x 10^10 tons a year (700 times more), so volcanoes add little to the CO2 rise.
Eruptions can cool the climate by about 0.3 C for about 3 years, but this effect is short-lived and does not offset long-term warming caused by the increase in CO2 from human activities.

questions.question: How many of the four statements describe glycogen? 1 The monomer is beta glucose; 2 It is made from two different types of polymer; 3 There are 1,4 and 1,6 glycosidic bonds; 4 It is insoluble. Options A 1, B 2, C 3, D 4.
questions.answer: B: 2 (statements 3 and 4).
steps: Statement 1 is false: the monomer of glycogen is alpha glucose, not beta glucose.
Statement 2 is false: glycogen is a single polymer of alpha glucose.
Statement 3 is true: 1,4 bonds form the chains and 1,6 bonds form the branches.
Statement 4 is true: glycogen is insoluble, so it stores glucose without changing water potential.
Two statements are correct, so the answer is B.

questions.question: Explain the changes in the concentrations of glycogen and glucose, using the graph.
questions.answer: Liver glycogen falls from about 3500 to about 2300 umol g^-1 over 48 h while plasma glucose rises from about 5 to about 200 umol cm^-3, because glycogen is broken down to glucose that enters the plasma.
steps: Glycogen in the liver falls, e.g. from about 3500 umol g^-1 at 0 h to about 2500 at 30 h and about 2300 at 48 h.
At the same time plasma glucose rises from about 5 to about 150 umol cm^-3 at 30 h and about 200 at 48 h.
The glycogen is hydrolysed (glycogenolysis) to glucose, which is released from the liver into the plasma.
The glucose raises the solute concentration of the blood, which lowers its freezing point and protects against freezing at -16 C.

questions.question: Calculate the percentage difference in the mean concentration of urea in plasma of Alaska wood frogs compared with Ohio wood frogs, using the table.
steps: Difference = 106 - 28 = 78 umol cm^-3.
Percentage difference compared with Ohio = 78 / 28 x 100 = 278.6%.
Alaska frogs have about 279% more urea (about 3.8 times as much).

questions.question: Explain why the data for the Alaska wood frogs are more reliable than the data for the Ohio wood frogs, using the standard deviations in the table.
questions.answer: The Alaska data are more reliable because their standard deviation is a smaller proportion of the mean (10 / 106 = 9.4%) than for Ohio (5 / 28 = 17.9%), so the values are less spread out.
steps: Standard deviation shows the spread of the data around the mean; a smaller spread relative to the mean means more reliable data.
Alaska: 10 / 106 x 100 = 9.4% of the mean.
Ohio: 5 / 28 x 100 = 17.9% of the mean, almost twice as variable, so the Ohio data are less reliable even though its absolute SD is lower.

questions.question: Explain why a high concentration of solutes in the plasma could protect the Alaska wood frogs in very cold temperatures.
questions.answer: High solute concentration lowers the freezing point of body fluids and water potential, so less ice forms and cells are protected from ice damage.
steps: Dissolved solutes lower the freezing point of the body fluids (plasma).
The fluids can therefore stay liquid at temperatures below 0 C.
Lower water potential also reduces the amount of ice that forms and the water lost to ice.
This protects cells from damage by ice crystals.

questions.question: Explain how these wood frogs evolved to occupy different niches in North America.
questions.answer: Random mutations gave variation; natural selection in cold Alaska and milder Ohio favoured different traits, so populations diverged into different niches.
steps: Mutations in frog populations produce random variation in traits such as solute concentration and glycogen storage.
Populations spread into different climates, e.g. cold Alaska and milder Ohio.
In each environment, natural selection favours the frogs with traits best suited to that niche, which survive and breed.
Over many generations the allele frequencies change, so each population adapts to its own niche.
Geographical isolation of the populations allows them to diverge further.

questions.question: State the meaning of the term biomass.
questions.answer: The mass of living material (organic matter) of organisms in a given area or group.
steps: Biomass is the mass of living organisms or organic material.
It can be measured as dry mass or as the mass of carbon in the organisms.
It is usually given for a particular area or group of organisms.
It measures how much matter is stored in living things.

questions.question: Calculate the percentage of biomass in organisms belonging to the domain Eukarya, using diagram A.
steps: Eukarya in diagram A: plants 450 + fungi 12 + protists 4 + animals 2 = 468 Gt C.
Total biomass = 7 (archaea) + 0.2 (viruses) + 70 (bacteria) + 468 = 545.2 Gt C.

questions.question: Suggest why scientists studied the distribution of biomass in groups of organisms rather than the number of individual organisms, using diagram A.
questions.answer: Organisms vary enormously in size, so counts are misleading; biomass shows the mass of matter and energy stored, allowing fair comparison between groups.
steps: Individual organisms vary greatly in size, e.g. bacteria are tiny while trees are huge.
Counting individuals gives a tiny bacterium the same weight as a large plant.
Biomass (mass of carbon) reflects the amount of matter and energy in each group.
So biomass allows a fair comparison of how much living material different groups contribute.

questions.question: Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of presenting data in Voronoi diagrams, using diagram B.
questions.answer: Advantage: many groups are shown at once and area is proportional to biomass; disadvantage: the shape has no meaning and exact values are hard to read.
steps: Advantage: one diagram shows the relative biomass of many groups together.
Area is proportional to biomass, so larger groups are easy to compare visually in diagram B.
Disadvantage: the shape of each polygon has no meaning, so it may mislead about other features.
Disadvantage: exact values are hard to read from areas, so it is less precise than a table or bar chart.

questions.question: Explain the distribution of biomass in marine, deep underground and land environments, using the Voronoi diagram and the graph.
questions.answer: Land holds most biomass (470 Gt C) because plants, which are 450 Gt C and all on land, dominate; deep underground biomass (70 Gt C) is almost all bacteria and archaea; marine biomass is only 6 Gt C and mostly animals and protists.
steps: Land has the most biomass (470 Gt C, about 86% of all biomass) because plants, the producers, make up 100% of plant biomass (450 Gt C) there, with plenty of light, water and carbon dioxide for photosynthesis, and fungi are about 97% on land.

Marine biomass is only 6 Gt C even though oceans are large, because the producers there are tiny phytoplankton with a short life and fast turnover, so little biomass exists at any one time; animals (about 76%) and protists (about 56%) are mostly marine consumers.

Deep underground biomass is 70 Gt C and about 88% of bacteria and archaea are found there; there is no light so no photosynthesis, so these prokaryotes use chemical energy or organic matter (chemosynthesis or decomposition) and live slowly in small numbers.
No plants are found underground or in deep water because they need light, and bacteria and archaea are found in all three environments.

questions.question: In 2017 the global seaweed harvest was 32.9 million tonnes, of which 96.6% was cultivated. Calculate the mass of cultivated seaweed, in standard form.
questions.answer: 3.18 x 10^7 tonnes.
steps: Write 32.9 million tonnes as 32.9 x 10^6 tonnes.
Multiply by 0.966: 32.9 x 0.966 = 31.78 (million tonnes).
Write in standard form: 31.78 x 10^6 = 3.18 x 10^7 tonnes.
The answer is slightly less than the total harvest, which fits 96.6% being cultivated.

questions.question: Which type of bond is broken in a water molecule during photosynthesis? A covalent, B glycosidic, C hydrogen, D ionic.
questions.answer: A: covalent.
steps: Photosynthesis splits water molecules (photolysis) to release hydrogen and oxygen.
The bonds broken are the strong bonds within the water molecule, i.e. the O-H bonds.
These are covalent bonds, in which atoms share electrons.
Hydrogen bonds act between molecules, not within them, so C is wrong.

questions.question: Which is a fuel that stores hydrogen in plants and seaweeds? A ATP, B glucose, C glycogen, D RuBisCO.
questions.answer: B: glucose.
steps: Hydrogen from water is combined with CO2 in the light-independent reactions.
This makes triose phosphate, which is converted into glucose.
Glucose is a fuel whose bonds store the hydrogen and energy, released in respiration.
Glycogen is the storage carbohydrate of animals and fungi, not plants; ATP is an energy carrier and RuBisCO is an enzyme.

questions.question: Which row of the table shows the reactions that combine hydrogen with carbon dioxide and release oxygen into the atmosphere?
questions.answer: C: hydrogen is combined with carbon dioxide in the light-independent reactions, and oxygen is released in the light-dependent reactions.
steps: Oxygen comes from photolysis of water, which occurs in the light-dependent reactions.
Hydrogen (as reduced NADP) is combined with carbon dioxide in the Calvin cycle, the light-independent reactions.
Only row C has both correct.

questions.question: Discuss the considerations for deciding whether large-scale seaweed production is suitable in Europe, using the two diagrams and own knowledge.
questions.answer: Large-scale seaweed farming could be suitable if the benefits (carbon absorption, food and raw materials, jobs, habitat) outweigh the costs (shading, noise, labour, transport and processing) after careful environmental assessment.
steps: Benefits: seaweed absorbs carbon dioxide by photosynthesis, which reduces atmospheric CO2; it needs no fresh water, fertiliser or farmland and gives food, feed and fuel; the suspended rows act as an artificial habitat that shelters fish and invertebrates and can increase biodiversity.
Labour: it provides jobs and income, but labour is costly in Europe and harvesting needs people, so it may be less economic than in Asia.
Absorption of light: dense rows shade the water below, reducing photosynthesis by phytoplankton and sea grasses and affecting the food chain.
Noise from boats and machinery can disturb marine animals such as fish and whales, and lines can entangle animals; the seaweed may also remove nutrients or spread disease.
Transport and processing need energy and facilities, which add costs and carbon emissions, so sites should be near ports and processing plants.
Conclusion: weigh human needs (food, jobs, carbon capture) against conservation by carrying out environmental impact assessments, small trials, monitoring and licensing before expanding.

questions.question: What is the difference in hydrogen ion concentration between a fore dune and a grey dune? Options: A 2 times more, B 2 times fewer, C 100 times more, D 100 times fewer.
questions.answer: D: a fore dune has 100 times fewer hydrogen ions than a grey dune.
steps: pH of fore dune = 8.5; pH of grey dune = 6.5, a difference of 2 pH units.
Hydrogen ion concentration = 10^-pH, so fore dune is 10^-8.5 and grey dune is 10^-6.5.
The ratio is 10^-8.5 / 10^-6.5 = 10^-2 = 1/100, so the fore dune has 100 times fewer.

questions.question: Calculate the percentage increase in the number of plant species on the grey dune compared with the fore dune.
steps: Species on the grey dune = 15; on the fore dune = 2.
Increase = 15 - 2 = 13.
Percentage increase = 13 / 2 x 100 = 650%.

questions.question: Explain the changes in the sand dunes with distance from the sea, using the table.
questions.answer: The dunes show primary succession: pioneer plants on the fore dune add organic matter, which deepens and enriches the soil and lowers its pH, so conditions become less harsh and more plant species can grow with distance from the sea.
steps: Close to the sea (fore dune) conditions are harsh: soil depth <0.5 cm, <1.0% organic matter, pH 8.5, over 97% bare ground, and only 2 species (pioneers such as sea rocket and saltwort that tolerate salt, wind and low nutrients).
The pioneers die and decompose, so organic matter increases (to 5.0% on the grey dune) and soil depth increases (8.0 cm); this holds more water and mineral ions.
Marram grass and other plants stabilise the sand, so bare ground falls from over 97% to 10% as plant cover increases.
Decomposition releases organic acids and carbonates are leached, so the pH falls from 8.5 to 6.5.

The improved soil and shelter allow more species to survive, so the number of species rises from 2 to 15 (650% increase), and these species outcompete the pioneers, giving a change in species at each stage towards a climax community of meadow plants.
Dunes further from the sea are older, so there has been more time for succession.

questions.question: Describe the conclusions that can be drawn from the graph of mean NPP above and below ground for fixed, semi-fixed and shifting dunes.
questions.answer: NPP is highest on fixed dunes and lowest on shifting dunes, and above-ground NPP is about 3 times the below-ground NPP in each type.
steps: Fixed dunes have the highest NPP: about 220 g m^-2 yr^-1 above ground and 70 below ground, then semi-fixed (about 125 and 45), then shifting (about 10 and 3).
NPP falls as the dunes become less stable, so stable, vegetated dunes support much more plant growth (about 22 times the above-ground NPP of shifting dunes).
In each type of dune, NPP is greater above ground than below ground (by about 3 times).
The error bars do not overlap between dune types, so the differences are likely to be real.

questions.question: Explain how the products of the light-independent reactions become NPP below ground.
questions.answer: Triose phosphate is made into sucrose and sent by phloem to the roots, where it is converted to starch and cellulose for growth and storage.
steps: Triose phosphate from the Calvin cycle is converted into glucose, then sucrose.
Sucrose is loaded into the phloem and moved by mass flow to the roots.
In the roots it is converted into starch for storage or cellulose and other compounds for new cells.
Some is used in respiration to release energy for growth; the new biomass stored below ground is the NPP.

questions.question: Give the meaning of the term habitat, illustrated with the organisms on the African plains (lions, giraffes, acacia trees).
questions.answer: A habitat is the place where an organism lives, e.g. the African plains where lions, giraffes and acacia trees are found.
steps: A habitat is the environment or place in which an organism normally lives.
It provides the food, shelter and conditions the organism needs to survive.
Example: the African plains are the habitat of lions, giraffes and acacia trees.
Different organisms can share a habitat but occupy different niches within it.

questions.question: Give the meaning of the term population, illustrated with the organisms on the African plains.
questions.answer: All the individuals of one species living in the same area at the same time, e.g. the lions of one pride on the plains.
steps: A population is all the members of one species in a given area.
They live at the same time and can interbreed.
Example: all the giraffes living in one part of the African plains form one population.
This is different from a community, which includes all the species present.

questions.question: Give the meaning of the term community, illustrated with lions, giraffes and acacia trees on the African plains.
questions.answer: All the populations of different species living and interacting in the same area, e.g. lions, giraffes and acacia trees on the plains.
steps: A community is all the populations of different species in one area.
The populations interact with each other, e.g. through predation and feeding.
Example: lions, giraffes and acacia trees form a community on the African plains.
The community together with its abiotic environment forms an ecosystem.

questions.question: Give the meaning of the term niche, illustrated with the trophic levels of lions, giraffes and acacia trees.
questions.answer: The role of an organism in its ecosystem, including its habitat, food and interactions, e.g. giraffes eat acacia leaves as primary consumers.
steps: A niche is the role an organism plays in its ecosystem.
It includes its habitat, what it eats and how it interacts with other species.
Example: acacia trees are producers, giraffes are primary consumers eating them, and lions are predators at a higher trophic level.
No two species occupy exactly the same niche in a stable community.

questions.question: Calculate the efficiency of energy transfer between trophic level one and trophic level two, using the diagram.
steps: Trophic level one has 534 223 kJ and trophic level two has 44 988 kJ.
Efficiency = energy in level 2 / energy in level 1 x 100.

questions.question: Which row of the table shows the colour of each of these seaweeds?
questions.answer: A: U. fasciata green, S. linifolium brown, C. officinalis red.
steps: U. fasciata has by far the most chlorophyll a and b, so chlorophyll dominates and it is green.
C. officinalis has almost no chlorophyll b and relatively more carotenoids, which fits a red seaweed.
S. linifolium has less chlorophyll and its carotenoids give it a brown colour.
Row A is the only row with green, brown and red in this order.

questions.question: Explain the role of chloroplast pigments in the light-dependent reactions of photosynthesis.
questions.answer: Pigments absorb light energy, which excites electrons that pass along the electron transport chain, producing ATP and reduced NADP.
steps: Chloroplast pigments such as chlorophyll absorb photons of light energy.
This energy excites electrons in the photosystem to a higher energy level.
The excited electrons pass along the electron transport chain and release energy.
This energy makes ATP and reduces NADP; the lost electrons are replaced by photolysis of water.

questions.question: Describe how GALP, produced in chloroplasts, is converted into protein.
questions.answer: GALP is converted to pyruvate and other intermediates, which gain amino groups from nitrogen to form amino acids; amino acids are joined by peptide bonds at ribosomes.
steps: GALP (triose phosphate) is converted to pyruvate through glycolysis, and then to intermediates of the Krebs cycle.
Nitrate ions taken up from the soil are reduced to ammonia, providing nitrogen.
The nitrogen is transferred (transamination) to these intermediates to form amino acids.
Amino acids are joined by peptide bonds at ribosomes during translation, forming protein.

questions.question: Comment on the statement that these seaweeds are a healthy, environmentally-friendly and economic food source, using the table and own knowledge.
questions.answer: Partly supported: the table shows useful protein, carbohydrate and antioxidants with little lipid, and seaweeds need no land or fertiliser, but data are only for two seaweeds and give no information on cost, toxins or vitamins.
steps: Healthy: lipid is low (2.96% and 2.16% of dry mass), protein is 9.56% and 14.89%, and carbohydrate is 23.70% and 25.03%.

Healthy: carotenoids, phenols and flavonoids are antioxidants that protect cells from free radicals; S. linifolium has more carotenoids (3.00 v 2.00) while U. fasciata has more phenols and flavonoids.
Environmentally friendly: seaweeds photosynthesise using sunlight and sea water, so need no farmland, fresh water or fertiliser, and they take up carbon dioxide.
Economic: they grow quickly and can be harvested cheaply, so should cost less than animal protein.

Limits: only two of the three seaweeds are in the table, antioxidant values are in arbitrary units, and there is no data on vitamins, minerals, heavy metals, digestibility or cost; wild harvesting could damage ecosystems.
Conclusion: the statement is supported in part but the evidence is incomplete.

questions.question: The smallest walnut has a volume of about 50 cm3. Calculate the approximate volume of the largest hazelnut using the formula given (pi = 3, l = length, w = width).
steps: With pi = 3, volume = 4/3 x 3 x l x w^2 = 4 x l x w^2.
The largest hazelnut is 2.5 cm long and 1.5 cm wide.

questions.question: Design a laboratory investigation to find out which of the three types of nut ground squirrels prefer to eat.
questions.answer: Offer equal masses of each nut type together, record the mass of each eaten over time, and repeat with replicates and controls.
steps: Use several ground squirrels, each in an identical cage with water available.
Offer equal masses of acorns, hazelnuts and walnuts together, so the squirrel can choose freely.
Weigh the nuts before and after a set time, recording the mass eaten of each type.
Repeat with different squirrels and include a control with no nuts to allow for loss, so means are reliable.
Keep all other conditions (light, temperature, time of day) the same.

questions.question: Predict the results of this investigation, giving reasons and using the information in the table.
questions.answer: Hazelnuts and walnuts will be eaten more than acorns, because they contain more energy per 100 g (2788 and 2822 kJ against 1619 kJ); hazelnuts may be chosen most because they are smaller and easier to carry in the pouches.
steps: Squirrels need to store as much energy as possible, so they should choose the nuts with the most energy: walnut 2822 and hazelnut 2788 kJ per 100 g, which are almost equal and about 1.7 times the energy of acorns (1619).
Acorns are predicted to be eaten least, as their energy content is much lower.
Walnuts are large (3.0 to 5.0 cm long, about 50 cm^3 or more) with a hard shell, so they take more effort to open and carry, which may make hazelnuts (1.5 to 2.5 cm) the first choice.
The result should be measured as the mass of each nut eaten, repeated with several squirrels.

questions.question: Suggest how ground squirrels evolved food pouches.
questions.answer: Random variation gave some squirrels larger pouches for storing food, so they survived winter and reproduced more, passing on the trait.
steps: Random mutations gave some squirrels slightly larger cheek pouches.
These squirrels could carry and store more nuts for the winter.
Squirrels with larger pouches survived winter better and reproduced more often.
The alleles for larger pouches were passed on, and over many generations the trait became common.

questions.question: Calculate the radius of a tree with a circumference of 8 m, giving your answer to two decimal places.
steps: Use the formula C = 2 pi r, so r = C / (2 pi).
Give to two decimal places: 1.27 m.
Check: 2 x pi x 1.27 = 7.98 m, which is close to 8 m.

questions.question: The increment borer was 1 m long and did not reach the middle of the trunk; T is the distance from its end to the middle. Calculate T as a percentage of the radius.
steps: The borer was inserted from the bark, so its 1 m length reaches 1 m towards the centre.
The distance left to the middle is T = radius - 1.00 m = 1.27 - 1.00 = 0.27 m (27 cm).
As a percentage of the radius: 0.27 / 1.27 x 100 = 21.3%.
This is the part of the radius that the core did not sample.

questions.question: Which row of the table shows the newest and oldest rings in this tree?
questions.answer: B: newest ring P, oldest ring S.
steps: Growth rings are added to the outside of the trunk each year, so the newest ring is at the bark; P is at the left-hand side of the trunk, at the outside.
The oldest ring is at the centre of the trunk, which is S.

questions.question: Explain how these core samples can be used to calculate the age of the tree, using the question and the diagram.
questions.answer: Each ring is one year of growth; aligned cores are counted from bark to centre, with any missing rings estimated, to give the total age.
steps: Each annual ring is one year of growth, seen as a band of wide and narrow rings.
Cores from different heights are matched by aligning the rings, giving a continuous sequence of years.
Count the rings from the bark (newest) to the centre (oldest) in the core that reaches the centre.
If no core reaches the centre, estimate the missing rings from ring width and the distance to the centre, then add them to give the age.

questions.question: Describe how the growth rate of this tree can be calculated.
questions.answer: Divide the radius (centre to bark) by the age in years, giving mean growth in cm per year.
steps: Measure the radius from the centre of the trunk to the bark, using the core samples.
Find the age of the tree in years by counting the rings.
Divide the radius by the age: growth rate = radius / age (cm per year).
Alternatively, measure the width of rings for different years to compare growth in each year.

questions.question: 113 gigatonnes of carbon in underground biomass is equivalent to the CO2 emitted by humans in 10 years; 1 gigatonne = 10^12 kg. Calculate the mass of CO2 produced by humans in one year, in standard form.
questions.answer: 1.13 x 10^13 kg per year.
steps: The CO2 emitted by humans in 10 years is equivalent to 113 Gt.
Divide by 10 for one year: 113 / 10 = 11.3 Gt per year.
Convert using 1 Gt = 10^12 kg: 11.3 x 10^12 kg.
Write in standard form: 1.13 x 10^13 kg, using the equivalence stated in the question.

questions.question: Describe how GALP produced in the leaves becomes incorporated into biomass in the roots.
questions.answer: GALP becomes sucrose, is loaded into the phloem and moved by mass flow to the roots, where it builds new cell material and is stored as starch.
steps: GALP (triose phosphate) is converted into glucose and then sucrose in the leaf.
Sucrose is actively loaded into the phloem sieve tubes by companion cells.
It is transported by mass flow from the leaves (source) to the roots (sink).
In the roots sucrose is unloaded and converted to starch for storage, or to cellulose and other molecules for growth, increasing root biomass.

questions.question: For each molecule in the table, mark which inorganic ion provides an atom found in the molecule.
questions.answer: Cellulose: neither nitrate nor phosphate; nucleic acid: both nitrate and phosphate; triglyceride: neither nitrate nor phosphate.
steps: Cellulose is a polymer of glucose, containing only carbon, hydrogen and oxygen, so it needs neither ion.
Nucleic acids contain nitrogen in their bases (from nitrate) and phosphorus in the sugar-phosphate backbone (from phosphate), so need both.
Triglycerides contain only carbon, hydrogen and oxygen, so neither ion.

questions.question: Discuss how the abiotic factors shown in the graphs could affect the proportion of biomass stored in the roots of plants in forests, shrublands and grasslands.
questions.answer: Temperature is the most important factor in forests and shrublands, and soil moisture in grasslands; water, temperature, soil nutrients and soil depth change how much carbon is allocated to roots, so the proportion differs between ecosystems.
steps: Yearly mean temperature has the highest relative importance in forests (1.0) and shrublands (1.0) and is high in grasslands (about 0.84); it affects enzyme activity, photosynthesis, respiration and decomposition, so it affects how much carbon plants make and how much they store in roots.

Soil moisture is most important in grasslands (1.0) and high in forests (about 0.9) but lower in shrublands (about 0.48); where water is short plants invest more biomass in roots to reach water, so roots hold a higher proportion of biomass.

The carbon : nitrogen ratio in soil is of medium importance in all three (about 0.44 to 0.52); a high ratio means little nitrate is available, so plants make more roots (and associated fungi) to absorb it.

Depth of soil is the least important in all three (0.40 in forests, 0.24 in shrublands, 0.20 in grasslands), but it matters most in forests because deeper soil allows larger root systems; tree density (about 0.36 to 0.60, a biotic factor) increases competition for water and nutrients, so more root biomass.
Evaluation: the graphs show importance not the direction of the effect, they do not give biomass values, and the factors interact.

questions.question: Where in the chloroplast is RuBisCO active? Options: A P, B Q, C R, D S.
questions.answer: B: Q (the stroma).
steps: RuBisCO fixes carbon dioxide in the Calvin cycle, the light-independent reactions.
Structure Q is the site of the light-independent reactions and is colourless, so it is the stroma.

questions.question: What is stored in structure S? A GALP, B lipid, C starch, D sucrose.
questions.answer: C: starch.
steps: S is the storage granule, 1 to 35 um in size, so it is a starch grain.
GALP and sucrose are not stored in chloroplast granules, and lipid is stored as small droplets.

questions.question: Where is GP (glycerate 3-phosphate) formed? Options: A P, B Q, C R, D S.
questions.answer: B: Q (the stroma).
steps: GP (glycerate 3-phosphate) is the first product when RuBP combines with carbon dioxide, catalysed by RuBisCO.
This happens in the Calvin cycle in the stroma, which is Q.

questions.question: Which is the correct order of size, smallest to largest, for the structures P, R and S? A PRS, B PSR, C RSP, D SRP.
questions.answer: A: P R S.
steps: P is a ribosome of about 20 nm = 0.02 um.
R is a thylakoid space, largest 4.35 x 10^-4 mm = 0.435 um (435 nm).
S is a starch grain of 1 to 35 um.
Smallest to largest: P (0.02 um), R (0.435 um), S (1 to 35 um).

questions.question: Which could be the units for the rate of photosynthesis? A mg CO2 produced mm-2 hr-1, B mg CO2 produced mm-1 hr-2, C mg CO2 used mm-2 hr-1, D mg CO2 used mm-1 hr-2.
questions.answer: C: mg CO2 used mm^-2 hr^-1.
steps: The rate of photosynthesis is the amount of CO2 used by the leaf per unit area per unit time.
Photosynthesis uses CO2, so the unit must say 'used', not 'produced' (A and B are wrong).
Rate per unit area is mm^-2, not mm^-1 as in B and D.
Per unit time is hr^-1, giving mg CO2 used mm^-2 hr^-1, which is option C.

questions.question: Compare and contrast the rate of photosynthesis of these two plant species at different temperatures.
questions.answer: Both rise to an optimum then fall, but Spartina has a much higher maximum (about 40 a.u. at about 35 C) than Leucopoa (about 16 a.u. at about 20-25 C), and Leucopoa is faster only below about 15 C.
steps: Similarity: both species show an increase in rate to a maximum then a decrease, as enzymes become less effective above the optimum.
Spartina rises steeply from about 10 a.u. at 10 C to about 40 a.u. at 35 C, whereas Leucopoa rises only slightly, from about 13 to about 16.5 a.u.
The optimum is higher for Spartina (about 35 C) than for Leucopoa (about 20-25 C).
Below about 15 C Leucopoa has the higher rate; above that Spartina is higher, and at 40 C it is about 36 a.u. against 9 a.u.

questions.question: Describe how a Q10 value for the rate of photosynthesis can be calculated using the graph.
questions.answer: Q10 = rate at (T + 10) divided by rate at T, using two temperatures 10 C apart on the graph.
steps: Choose a starting temperature T on the graph and read the rate of photosynthesis there.
Find the rate at a temperature 10 C higher (T + 10) on the same line.
Divide the rate at T + 10 by the rate at T.
The result is the Q10, showing how much the rate increases for each 10 C rise.

questions.question: Explain in which of the two regions, Wheatland or Pole Mountain, Spartina is most likely to grow, using both graphs.
questions.answer: Wheatland: Spartina needs high temperatures (optimum about 35 C) and Wheatland is warmer, with maximum temperatures of 27-31 C from June to August.
steps: Spartina has its highest rate of photosynthesis (about 40 a.u.) at about 35 C and a low rate (about 10 a.u.) at 10-15 C.
Wheatland has maximum temperatures above 20 C from May to September, reaching about 31 C in July, close to the optimum for Spartina.
Pole Mountain never exceeds about 24 C and is below 15 C for most of the year, where Spartina photosynthesises slowly, so it would grow poorly there.

questions.question: State the term used to describe climate change caused by human activity.
questions.answer: Anthropogenic climate change.
steps: Anthropogenic means caused by human activity.
Climate change caused by humans is called anthropogenic climate change.
It is contrasted with natural climate change, which has other causes.
It is the term used for human-driven global warming.

questions.question: Explain why some people consider the claim that human-caused climate change is responsible for the increase in forest fires to be controversial.
questions.answer: Climate varies naturally and fires occur naturally, so it is hard to prove the human contribution; the evidence and models are uncertain.
steps: Climate naturally varies over long periods, and forest fires have always occurred.
It is difficult to separate the human contribution from natural causes such as lightning and drought.
Data and models are uncertain or limited for particular regions and events.
Some people hold different views or interests, so the evidence is debated.

questions.question: Discuss the effects that forest fires have on the local atmosphere and local biodiversity, in the short term and the long term.
questions.answer: Short term: smoke and CO2 pollute the air and animals and plants die; long term: succession and recovery of biodiversity and carbon stores, though recovery takes decades.
steps: Short term: fires release CO2, carbon monoxide and smoke particles into the local atmosphere, reducing air quality.
Short term: plants and animals are killed or displaced, reducing biodiversity and destroying habitat.
Short term: loss of tree cover reduces the CO2 absorbed by photosynthesis and removes shade.
Long term: nutrients from the ash enrich the soil, and pioneer species colonise the burnt area.
Long term: succession leads over decades to a new community, and biodiversity and carbon stores slowly recover, depending on fire frequency.

questions.question: Explain why the changes to the environment caused by climate change need to be considered when selecting tree species for reforestation.
questions.answer: Climate change alters temperature, rainfall and drought patterns, so trees must tolerate future conditions or the plantings will fail.
steps: Climate change raises temperatures and alters rainfall and the frequency of drought and flooding.
Tree species not adapted to these new conditions may die or grow poorly.
Species should be chosen for tolerance of future conditions, such as drought or heat, so they survive.
Suitable species make the reforestation successful and keep the carbon store and habitat in the long term.

questions.question: Which gases could be responsible for the temperature changes shown? A carbon dioxide and methane, B carbon dioxide and oxygen, C carbon dioxide, methane and oxygen, D methane and oxygen.
questions.answer: A: carbon dioxide and methane.
steps: Carbon dioxide and methane are greenhouse gases that absorb infrared radiation.
Oxygen does not absorb infrared radiation significantly, so it is not a greenhouse gas.
Options B, C and D each include oxygen, so they are wrong.
Option A contains only the two greenhouse gases.

questions.question: What is the estimated change in the mean surface temperature of the Earth in 2030? Options A 1.3, B 1.1, C 0.8, D 0.2.
questions.answer: A: 1.3 C (extending the upward trend of the graph to 2030).
steps: The mean temperature change rises from about 0 C in 1975 to about 1.0 C in 2017, a rate of about 0.024 C per year, and the rate is not slowing.
Extending the trend line to 2030 adds about 13 x 0.024 = 0.3 C to the 2017 value of 1.0 C.
The estimated change in 2030 is therefore about 1.3 C, option A (the other options are below the 2017 value or extend the line too little).

questions.question: Which row of the table describes the passage of ultraviolet light and infrared radiation, reflected from the Earth's surface, through gases in the atmosphere?
questions.answer: B: ultraviolet light passes through and infrared radiation does not pass through.
steps: Short-wavelength ultraviolet light from the Sun passes through the atmosphere to the Earth's surface.
Infrared radiation re-emitted from the Earth is absorbed by greenhouse gases such as carbon dioxide and methane, so it does not pass through, which causes the greenhouse effect.
Only row B shows this.

questions.question: Which of the following involves the study of tree rings? A dendrochronology, B entomology, C epigenetics, D proteomics.
questions.answer: A: dendrochronology.
steps: Dendrochronology is the scientific dating of tree rings.
Entomology is the study of insects.
Epigenetics is the study of heritable changes in gene expression without changes to the DNA sequence.
Proteomics is the study of the full set of proteins, so option A is correct.

questions.question: Explain why the width of tree rings produced in 1970 would be different from the width of tree rings produced in 2010.
questions.answer: Ring width reflects annual growth, which depends on temperature, rainfall and light; these differed between 1970 and 2010 as the climate changed.
steps: The width of each annual ring depends on how much the tree grew that year.
Growth depends on conditions such as temperature, water availability and the length of the growing season.
Climate change has changed temperatures and rainfall between 1970 and 2010.
Different conditions in each year gave different amounts of growth, so the rings differ in width.

questions.question: Explain why this diagram is described as a model of the effects of an increase in temperature.
questions.answer: It is a simplified representation of real effects that predicts likely outcomes from assumptions and data, since the future cannot be tested directly.
steps: A model is a simplified representation of a real system or process.
It shows likely effects of a temperature rise before those effects have happened.
It is based on assumptions and data, so it predicts rather than measures.
It can be tested and refined as new evidence becomes available.

questions.question: Calculate the percentage increase in the population exposed to drought if the temperature increases by 2 C rather than 1.5 C. Assume the bars are drawn to scale.
steps: The bar for the population exposed to drought is about 48 mm (1.5 C) and about 64 mm (2 C) long on the page, measured from the axis.
Increase = 64 - 48 = 16.
Percentage increase = 16 / 48 x 100 = 33% (one third more).

questions.question: Discuss the possible impacts of planting forests or crops on global warming, biodiversity and the local population, using the leaf area data for China and India.
questions.answer: Forests store more carbon and support more biodiversity than crops, which store less carbon and support fewer habitats; local people gain timber or food and income in different ways.
steps: Leaf area rose by 0.5 million km2; China's 25% is 0.125 million km2, half forest and half crops (0.0625 each).
India's 7% is 0.035 million km2, all planted as crops.
Forests store more carbon in biomass and soil than crops, so they reduce global warming more.
Crops are harvested and tilled, releasing carbon, and monocultures support less biodiversity than forest.
Forests provide timber, shade and water regulation for local people, while crops give food and income; both can displace other land uses and wildlife.

questions.question: Calculate the rate of oxygen production at 1200 seconds for C. pyrenoidosa with PBF attached.
questions.answer: About 0.07 nmol s^-1 (accept about 0.06 to 0.08).
steps: Draw a tangent to the curve for C. pyrenoidosa with PBF attached at 1200 s, where about 148 nmol of oxygen has been produced.
Take two points on the tangent, e.g. about 121 nmol at 800 s and about 175 nmol at 1600 s.

questions.question: Explain the effect PBF has on the production of oxygen by the algae.
questions.answer: PBF increases oxygen production: with PBF about 178 nmol is made in 1800 s against about 66 nmol without it (about 2.7 times more), because PBF absorbs green light that chlorophyll absorbs poorly.
steps: With PBF attached, the algae produce more oxygen at every time, reaching about 178 nmol at 1800 s compared with about 66 nmol without PBF, which stops rising after 1200 s.
PBF absorbs green light, which chlorophyll absorbs poorly, and passes this energy on, so more light energy is available for the light-dependent reactions.
More photolysis of water releases more oxygen, and more ATP and reduced NADP are made.
PBF alone produces almost no oxygen (about 4 nmol), so the extra oxygen is made by the algae and not by PBF itself.

questions.question: Explain why C. pyrenoidosa with PBF attached increased in mass more than C. pyrenoidosa without PBF over 20 days.
questions.answer: PBF absorbs extra light energy, so more photosynthesis makes more glucose, which is used to build more biomass.
steps: PBF absorbs green light that the algae would otherwise not use.
More light energy is absorbed, so more light-dependent reactions occur.
More ATP and reduced NADP are made, so more CO2 is fixed in the light-independent reactions.
More glucose and other organic molecules are made, which are used for growth and increase dry mass.

questions.question: In 2020 Thailand produced 4.37 million tonnes of rubber. Estimate the mass of rubber produced in Thailand in 2019, using the graph.
questions.answer: About 4.8 million tonnes (4.8 x 10^6 tonnes).
steps: Measure the height of each bar from the axis: 2019 is about 285 mm and 2020 about 258 mm on the page (about 1.1 times taller).
2019 mass = 4.37 million x 285 / 258 = 4.84 million tonnes.
So the estimate is about 4.8 x 10^6 tonnes (accept about 4.7 to 5.0 million).

questions.question: Explain how the cells in the trunk are able to synthesise the rubber molecule shown in the diagram, using GALP produced in the leaves, with the diagram and own knowledge.
questions.answer: GALP is transported to the trunk and converted to acetyl units and then isoprene units, which polymerise into rubber (poly-isoprene).
steps: GALP (triose phosphate) from the leaves is transported to the trunk, as sucrose in the phloem.
In the cells GALP is converted via pyruvate to acetyl units (2 carbons).
Acetyl units are combined to make 5-carbon isoprene building blocks, e.g. via the mevalonate pathway.
The isoprene units (the molecule in the diagram) are joined by enzymes into a long chain, the polymer rubber.

questions.question: Explain how dendrochronology could be used to determine the age of a rubber tree that is still producing rubber.
questions.answer: Take a core from the trunk with an increment borer and count the annual rings from bark to centre, without felling the tree.
steps: Use an increment borer to take a core sample from the trunk; this does not kill the tree.
Each annual ring is one year of growth, seen as a band of wide and narrow rings.
Count the rings from the bark to the centre of the core.
If the core does not reach the centre, estimate the missing rings from ring width to get the age.

questions.question: The mud core has a diameter of 80 mm and a length of 900 mm. Using V = pi r^2 l and pi = 3.142, which is the volume? A 4524 cm3, B 4525 cm3, C 18 097 cm3, D 18 098 cm3.
steps: Convert to cm: radius = 80 mm / 2 = 40 mm = 4 cm; length = 900 mm = 90 cm.
Apply V = pi r^2 l = 3.142 x 4^2 x 90.
Rounded down to a whole number this is 4524 cm3, which is option A.

questions.question: Calculate how many years the plants producing type D pollen grains were present in this rainforest, using the scale diagram.
questions.answer: About 750 years (accept about 700 to 800).
steps: The whole core covers 2700 years and is about 366 mm long on the page (present day to 2700 years ago), so 1 mm = 2700 / 366 = 7.4 years.
The bracket for type D is about 101 mm long.
Time = 101 x 7.4 = about 750 years.

questions.question: Explain the distribution of the three types of pollen grain in this mud column, using the diagram.
questions.answer: The pollen types are in different but overlapping layers: F deepest (oldest), D in the middle and E highest (youngest), showing that the plants in the rainforest changed over about 2700 years.
steps: Mud and pollen build up in layers with the oldest at the bottom, so deeper pollen is older; pollen is preserved in the waterlogged, oxygen-poor mud.
Type F is found lowest, about 2200 to 1200 years ago, so those plants were present first; type D is in the middle, about 1550 to 800 years ago; type E is highest, about 1250 to 600 years ago.

The overlaps show that plants with different pollen grew at the same time, but each type appears and later disappears, so the community changed (succession or a response to a changing climate or human activity).
There is no pollen of these types in the top layer (the last 600 years or so), so the plants that produced them are no longer present in significant numbers.

questions.question: Which diagram shows a mononucleotide of DNA?
questions.answer: C
steps: A mononucleotide has a pentose sugar with a base attached to carbon 1 and a phosphate attached to carbon 5 (through carbon 4).
In C the base and phosphate are both bonded to the sugar, on the two carbons that are either side of the ring oxygen (not adjacent).
A and B have the phosphate or base joined to the other one, not to the sugar, and in D the phosphate is on the carbon next to the base carbon, so only C is correct.

questions.question: Name the bond that joins nucleotides together in a strand of DNA.
questions.answer: Phosphodiester bond.
steps: Nucleotides are joined in a strand by condensation reactions.
A bond forms between the phosphate group of one nucleotide and the sugar of the next.
This bond is a phosphodiester bond, forming the sugar-phosphate backbone.
Phosphodiester bonds are covalent and strong, so the backbone is stable.

questions.question: Explain the positive correlation between temperature and the length of young lizards, which could be due to enzyme activity.
questions.answer: Higher temperature increases enzyme activity and metabolic rate up to the optimum, so growth processes happen faster and young lizards grow longer.
steps: Lizards cannot regulate their body temperature, so it matches the surroundings.
Higher temperature gives molecules more kinetic energy, so enzyme and substrate collide more often.
Enzyme-controlled reactions such as respiration and protein synthesis speed up, up to the optimum temperature.
Faster metabolism gives more energy and materials for growth, so the young lizards grow longer.

questions.question: Describe the relationship between the percentage change in abundance of lizards and the length of young lizards, using the graph.
questions.answer: A negative relationship: longer young lizards are linked with a larger decrease in abundance (about 51 mm at -65% to about 44.5 mm at +100%), and the curve levels off above about +60%.
steps: As the percentage change in abundance increases from about -65% to +100%, the length of young lizards decreases from about 51 mm to about 44.5 mm (negative correlation).
The decrease is steepest at the left (from about 51 to 46 mm between -65% and 0%) and flattens at the right (about 44.5 mm from +60% to +100%).

questions.question: Explain why the abundance of the longer lizards is affected by the number of cell divisions taking place as they grow, using all the information.
questions.answer: Each cell division shortens telomeres; faster-growing (longer) lizards divide more, so their telomeres shorten faster, cells die sooner and survival falls.
steps: Each time DNA is replicated, the telomeres at chromosome ends become shorter.
Longer young lizards have grown faster and so have undergone more cell divisions.
Their telomeres shorten more, and when they are too short the cell dies.
Fewer functioning cells may reduce survival, which changes the abundance of these lizards.

questions.question: State what is meant by the term anthropogenic climate change.
questions.answer: Long-term change in global climate caused by human activities, mainly greenhouse gas emissions from burning fossil fuels and land-use change.
steps: Anthropogenic means caused by human activity.
Climate change means long-term change in global temperature and weather patterns.
Human activities such as burning fossil fuels and deforestation release greenhouse gases.
These gases enhance the greenhouse effect and cause global warming.

questions.question: Name two greenhouse gases.
questions.answer: Carbon dioxide and methane (nitrous oxide or water vapour are also acceptable).
steps: Carbon dioxide is released by burning fossil fuels and by deforestation.
Methane is released by livestock, rice fields and landfill.
Nitrous oxide is released from fertilisers and is also a greenhouse gas.
Any two of these (CO2, methane, nitrous oxide, water vapour) are acceptable.

questions.question: Explain the role of greenhouse gases in climate change.
questions.answer: Greenhouse gases absorb infrared radiation emitted from the Earth and re-emit it, trapping heat in the atmosphere and warming the planet.
steps: Short-wave sunlight passes through the atmosphere and warms the Earth's surface.
The Earth emits longer-wavelength infrared radiation.
Greenhouse gases absorb this infrared and re-emit it in all directions, some back towards the surface.
This traps heat, so more greenhouse gas means more warming (global warming).

questions.question: Explain the relative contribution of each source of greenhouse gas emissions, using the pie chart and own knowledge.
questions.answer: Energy supply (25.9%) is the largest source because of burning fossil fuels; industry (19.4%), forestry (17.4%), agriculture (13.5%), transport (13.1%), buildings (7.9%) and waste (2.8%) follow, each releasing CO2, methane or nitrous oxide in different ways.
steps: Energy supply, the largest contributor (25.9%), comes from burning coal, oil and gas in power stations, which releases carbon dioxide; industry (19.4%) releases CO2 from fuel use, cement and chemical manufacture.
Forestry (17.4%) is high because deforestation removes trees that absorb CO2 by photosynthesis, and burning or decay of the wood releases CO2.
Agriculture (13.5%) releases methane from cattle and rice fields, and nitrous oxide from fertilisers and soils.
Transport (13.1%) releases CO2 from burning petrol, diesel and aviation fuel; buildings (7.9%) release CO2 from burning fuels for heating and cooking (electricity use is counted under energy supply).

Waste and wastewater (2.8%) is the smallest, from methane produced by anaerobic decay in landfill and sewage; the three main gases (CO2, CH4, N2O) absorb infrared radiation and add to the greenhouse effect.

questions.question: Calculate the total volume of one E. huxleyi, in mm3, using the dimensions shown in the diagram.
steps: The cell is 50 um across and the plates are 12 um thick on each side, so the total diameter = 50 + 12 + 12 = 74 um.
Radius = 37 um = 0.037 mm.

questions.question: One E. huxleyi can contain 12 plates and each plate takes 75 minutes to produce, one at a time. Calculate the number of hours to produce 12 plates.
questions.answer: 15 hours.
steps: Total time = 12 plates x 75 minutes per plate = 900 minutes.
Divide by 60 minutes per hour: 900 / 60.
The plates are made one at a time, so the times add up.

questions.question: Describe how scientists could show that plates shed into the water can attach to other E. huxleyi cells.
questions.answer: Label the shed plates with a fluorescent or radioactive marker, add them to cultures of cells, then detect the label on the cells with a microscope or detector.
steps: Collect plates shed into the water and label them with a fluorescent or radioactive marker.
Add the labelled plates to a culture of E. huxleyi cells.
After a set time, wash the cells to remove plates that have not attached.
Detect the label on the cells with a fluorescence microscope or radioactivity detector, comparing with a control that has no labelled plates.

questions.question: Explain the possible impact that virus-infected E. huxleyi producing dense marine snow could have on global warming and the effects of climate change.
questions.answer: Infected cells sink as dense marine snow, moving carbon to the deep ocean and reducing atmospheric CO2, but dying cells also photosynthesise less, so the overall effect is uncertain.
steps: Infected E. huxleyi produce a glue that binds many cells and plates into dense marine snow.
Marine snow sinks, moving carbon from surface waters to the deep ocean and sediments.
This removes carbon from the surface carbon cycle, so less CO2 returns to the atmosphere, reducing the greenhouse effect.
However, infected and dying cells photosynthesise less, so less CO2 is absorbed from the water.
Making calcium carbonate plates releases CO2, so fewer plates would mean less CO2 released locally.
Overall the effect on warming depends on this balance, with sinking carbon likely to slow climate change over time.

questions.question: Which process can be used to separate chloroplast pigments according to their solubility? A chromatography, B dendrochronology, C gel electrophoresis, D polymerase chain reaction.
questions.answer: A: chromatography.
steps: Chromatography separates substances as they move through a stationary phase in a solvent.
Pigments move at different rates depending on their solubility in the solvent and their attraction to the paper.
Dendrochronology dates tree rings and PCR copies DNA, so they are not separation methods.
Gel electrophoresis separates molecules by charge and size, not by solubility.

questions.question: Compare and contrast the types of chloroplast pigment found in the seaweeds with those found in the spinach, using the diagram of results.
questions.answer: All three contain chlorophyll a, beta-carotene and a xanthophyll, but spinach also has chlorophyll b and three xanthophylls, which the seaweeds lack, and the brown seaweed has extra pigments P and Q.
steps: Similarity: all three have a band for chlorophyll a at the same height and a faint band for beta-carotene near the solvent front.
