Difference: spinach has a chlorophyll b band and three xanthophyll bands, whereas neither seaweed has chlorophyll b and the seaweeds show only one band at the xanthophyll level.
Difference: the brown seaweed has two further bands, pigment P (between chlorophyll a and the xanthophyll) and pigment Q (near the origin), which are not found in spinach or the red seaweed.

questions.question: Describe how the student could identify pigment P using this method.
questions.answer: Calculate the Rf value of pigment P (distance moved by pigment divided by distance moved by solvent front) and compare it with known standard pigments run under the same conditions.
steps: Mark the origin line and measure the distance from the origin to the centre of the spot for pigment P.
Measure the distance from the origin to the solvent front.
Calculate Rf = distance moved by pigment / distance moved by solvent front.
Compare the Rf value with those of known standard pigments (e.g. chlorophyll a, chlorophyll b, carotene) run under identical conditions.
A matching Rf value suggests that pigment P is that known pigment.

questions.question: Which row of the table shows the light that green seaweed can absorb?
questions.answer: C: green light cannot be absorbed, red light can be absorbed.
steps: Green seaweed contains chlorophyll, which absorbs red and blue light strongly.
Chlorophyll reflects green light, so green light is not absorbed (it is why the seaweed looks green).
Only row C shows green light 'cannot absorb' and red light 'can absorb'.

questions.question: Explain the positions of the brown and red seaweeds on the submerged rock, using the diagram of light penetration.
questions.answer: Red light only penetrates near the surface, and green and blue light reach deeper; brown seaweed grows deeper than green seaweed and red seaweed deepest, as their pigments can absorb the green and blue light that reaches those depths.
steps: Red light is absorbed by the water near the surface, so green seaweed (chlorophyll absorbing red and blue light) grows in the shallowest zone.
Green and blue light penetrate deeper, so the brown seaweed in the middle zone has different pigments (such as pigment P and carotenoids) that absorb blue and green light.
The red seaweed is deepest because its pigments absorb the blue and green light that penetrates furthest, so it can still photosynthesise where little red light reaches.

questions.question: State the meaning of the term sympatric speciation.
questions.answer: Formation of a new species from a population living in the same geographical area, due to reproductive isolation.
steps: Speciation is the formation of a new species from an existing one.
Sympatric means living in the same geographical area.
A subpopulation becomes reproductively isolated from the rest, e.g. by using a different host or breeding time.
Over generations the subpopulation diverges genetically until it can no longer interbreed with the original population.

questions.question: Which row of the table represents sympatric speciation, where dark grey shapes are the original species and light grey shapes the new species?
questions.answer: D
steps: Sympatric speciation happens within the same area, with no geographical separation of the population.
In row D a new (light grey) species arises inside the original (dark grey) population, in the same area, and remains within it.
In A the population is split by a barrier and in B and C part of the population moves away, which are allopatric (geographical) types.

questions.question: Suggest two adaptations needed for the change in behaviour of the hawthorn flies that started laying eggs in apples.
questions.answer: A preference for the smell of apples (chemoreceptors) and an ovipositor suited to laying eggs in apple flesh.
steps: Flies need to detect apple odours and be attracted to them, so they need suitable chemoreceptors and behaviour.
Females need an ovipositor (egg-laying structure) of suitable length and shape to lay eggs in apple flesh.
Egg-laying must be timed to match when apples are on the tree.
Larvae must be able to digest and develop in apple tissue.

questions.question: Explain what had to occur for the changes in these flies to be inherited.
questions.answer: A genetic change (mutation) had to occur in the gametes (germ line) so that the allele was passed to offspring.
steps: The change in behaviour must have a genetic basis: a mutation in the DNA.
The mutation must occur in the cells that make gametes (the germ line) to be inherited.
Flies carrying the allele must mate and produce offspring.
The offspring inherit the allele, which is then passed on in later generations.

questions.question: Explain why it is an advantage for the hawthorn fly and the apple maggot fly to lay their eggs in the fruits of different plants.
questions.answer: It reduces competition for food between the larvae of the two species and reduces the chance of interbreeding.
steps: Larvae feed inside the fruit, so each fruit supports only a limited number of maggots.
Laying in different fruits means the two species do not compete for the same food.
Each species can exploit a separate food source, so more individuals survive.
It also reduces mating between the two species, keeping them separate.

questions.question: Suggest how these flies became reproductively isolated, using the diagram of fruit types and fruiting times.
questions.answer: Apples and hawthorn berries fruit at different times of the year and on different host plants, so the two fly groups rarely meet and mate.
steps: Apples and hawthorn berries are produced at different times of year, as shown in the diagram.
Flies emerging from each fruit are therefore active at different times.
Each fly group mainly lays eggs in its own host plant, so they are found in different places.
With less mating between the groups, gene flow stops and they become separate species.

questions.question: Which row of the table shows the products of the light-dependent reactions that are used in the light-independent reactions?
questions.answer: D: ATP from non-cyclic photophosphorylation and reduced NADP.
steps: The light-independent reactions use ATP and reduced NADP made in the light-dependent reactions.
Reduced NADP is made only in non-cyclic photophosphorylation (cyclic makes ATP only), so only row D is correct.

questions.question: Simple sugars have the formula CnH2nOn. Name the inorganic molecule that provides each element: C, H and O.
questions.answer: C from carbon dioxide; H from water (carried by reduced NADP); O from carbon dioxide and water.
steps: Carbon in simple sugars is fixed from carbon dioxide by RuBisCO in the Calvin cycle.
Hydrogen comes from water: it is split in photolysis and carried by reduced NADP.
Oxygen in the sugar comes from carbon dioxide (and water), since the oxygen in CO2 is retained.
So the inorganic sources are carbon dioxide for C, water for H, and carbon dioxide or water for O.

questions.question: Describe three conclusions about the differences in the effect of temperature on the rate of photosynthesis in C3 and C4 plants, using the graph.
questions.answer: C4 plants have a higher maximum rate (about 36 a.u. against about 24 a.u.) at a higher optimum (about 35 C against about 27 C), and fall more slowly at high temperature, whereas C3 plants are faster below about 20 C.
steps: The maximum rate of photosynthesis in C4 plants is about 36 a.u., higher than in C3 plants (about 24 a.u.).
The optimum temperature is higher for C4 plants (about 35 C) than for C3 plants (about 27 C).
Below about 20 C (where the curves cross, at about 22 a.u.) C3 plants have the higher rate; above about 20 C the C4 plants are higher.
The rate falls more slowly at high temperature in C4 plants (about 27 a.u. at 45 C) than in C3 plants (about 8 a.u. at 45 C).

questions.question: Calculate the Q10 for the enzymes in C4 plants, using the formula and giving your answer as a whole number.
steps: For C4 plants, the rate at 10 C is about 6 a.u. (R_t).
The rate at 20 C is about 22 a.u. (R_t+10).
Q10 = 22 / 6 = 3.7 = 4 to the nearest whole number.

questions.question: Give the meaning of the term habitat, with an example from this rainforest food chain.
questions.answer: A habitat is the place where an organism lives, e.g. the rainforest trees where slender lorises live.
steps: Habitat is the place or environment where an organism lives.
It provides the food, shelter and conditions the organism needs.
Example: slender lorises live in the trees of the Southeast Asian rainforest.
The rainforest is the habitat of all the organisms in this food chain.

questions.question: Give the meaning of the term population, with an example from this food chain.
questions.answer: All the individuals of one species living in the same area at the same time, e.g. a group of slender lorises in one part of the rainforest.
steps: A population is all the members of one species in an area at a given time.
The members can interbreed with each other.
Example: all the slender lorises living in one part of the rainforest.
This is one population within the larger rainforest community.

questions.question: Give the meaning of the term community, with an example from this food chain.
questions.answer: All the populations of different species living and interacting in the same area, e.g. slender lorises, Bengal tigers and other species in the rainforest.
steps: A community is all the populations of different species in an area.
These populations interact through feeding and other relationships.
Example: slender lorises, Bengal tigers and other species living in the same rainforest.
The community together with the abiotic environment forms an ecosystem.

questions.question: Explain how the niche of the slender loris affects the distribution and abundance of Bengal tigers, using the food chain.
questions.answer: The slender loris is the food of tigers, so tigers are found only where lorises live (in the rainforest trees) and the number of tigers depends on how many lorises there are.
steps: In the food chain the Bengal tiger (trophic level 3) feeds on the slender loris (level 2), so the loris is part of the tiger's niche (its food supply).
The loris lives in trees and feeds on young leaves, so the tiger's distribution is limited to the places in the rainforest where lorises and their food are found.
Only about 10% of energy passes from one trophic level to the next, so the loris population can support only a small number of tigers; if loris numbers fall, tiger abundance falls.

questions.question: Explain how the age of a tree in a rainforest can be determined without cutting it down.
questions.answer: Take a core with an increment borer and count the annual growth rings (dendrochronology).
steps: Use an increment borer to take a thin core from the trunk; the tree survives.
Each annual ring is one year of growth.
Count the rings from the bark to the centre of the core to find the age.
If the core does not reach the centre, estimate the missing rings from the ring width.

questions.question: Calculate the mean drop in height of the glacier from 1980 to 2000, giving suitable units.
questions.answer: 0.3 m per year (m yr^-1)
steps: The decrease in height from 1980 to 2000 is 6 m (from 0 to -6 m).
The time taken is 20 years.
Mean drop = 6 / 20 = 0.3 m per year.

questions.question: Explain why the decrease in height is greater from 1995 to 2000 than from 1980 to 1985.
questions.answer: Warming increases over time, so melting speeds up; less ice leaves darker ground exposed, which absorbs more heat (positive feedback).
steps: Global temperatures rose over this period, so the rate of ice melting increased.
As the glacier thins and retreats, more ground is exposed or the remaining ice is thinner, and it melts faster.
Exposed darker surfaces absorb more heat than ice (lower albedo), causing more melting (positive feedback).
So the cumulative effect of warming makes the loss much larger in the later years.

questions.question: Which letter on the diagram indicates the location of pioneer species only? A P, B Q, C R, D S.
questions.answer: A: P (the zone nearest the glacier, exposed most recently).
steps: Succession starts with pioneer species on newly exposed ground, so they are found alone where the ground has been exposed for the shortest time.
Zone P is the one nearest the front of the glacier, so it is the youngest ground; Q, R and S are further away and older, where other plants as well as pioneers occur.

questions.topic: Term For Soil Change Over Time
questions.question: Which term describes the changes in soil conditions and organisms with time? A anthropogenic, B evolution, C speciation, D succession.
questions.answer: D: succession.
steps: Changes in soil and organisms over time after ground is exposed are called succession.
Succession is the gradual change in the community of a habitat over time.
Anthropogenic means caused by humans, which is not the case here.
Evolution and speciation describe genetic change in populations, not community change over time.

questions.question: Explain the variations in soil conditions and the organisms found at different distances from the front edge of the glacier, using the table and graphs.
questions.answer: This is primary succession: ground exposed longest is furthest from the glacier, where pioneers are replaced by small then large plants as soil builds up, so diversity peaks at about 2000 years and then falls, while the soil C : N ratio changes from 9.8 to a maximum of 11.6.
steps: Pioneer species colonise bare ground first (probability about 0.8 at about 500 years) and add organic matter; they decline to almost zero by about 5000 years as they are outcompeted by plants better suited to the improved soil.
As organic matter accumulates and nitrogen is fixed, soil depth and fertility increase, so small plants peak (about 0.85 at about 2000 years) and large plants increase to about 0.87 by 5000 years.
Plant diversity rises quickly to a maximum of about 34 a.u. at about 1500 to 2000 years because more species can colonise the improved soil and there are many niches.
Diversity then falls to about 22 a.u. at 5000 years as large dominant plants shade and outcompete the others, giving a climax community.

The carbon : nitrogen ratio rises from 9.8 (under 200 years) to 11.6 (2000 years) as plant litter adds carbon faster than nitrogen is added, then falls to 10.7 and 10.3 as decomposition releases nitrogen and nitrogen-fixing organisms add more nitrogen.

questions.question: Textile waste was 92 million tonnes in 2022 and is expected to be 134 million tonnes a year by 2030. Calculate the increase, in standard form.
questions.answer: 4.2 x 10^7 tonnes.
steps: Increase = 134 million - 92 million = 42 million tonnes.
Convert to standard form: 42 x 10^6 = 4.2 x 10^7 tonnes.
Check: 92 million + 42 million = 134 million, which matches the 2030 figure.
The increase is an extra 42 million tonnes of waste produced each year.

questions.question: Which term describes the effect of human activity on the environment? A antigenic, B anthropogenic, C epigenetic, D polygenic.
questions.answer: B: anthropogenic.
steps: Anthropogenic means caused or produced by human activity.
Antigenic relates to antigens and immunity, not the environment.
Epigenetic relates to changes in gene expression without changes to the DNA sequence.
Polygenic relates to traits controlled by many genes, so B is the correct term.

questions.question: Give the meaning of the term sustainable as used in this context of textile production.
questions.answer: Meeting current textile needs without harming the environment or reducing the resources available for future generations.
steps: Sustainable means producing without depleting resources faster than they can be replaced.
It means reducing waste, pollution and carbon emissions.
Textiles should meet present needs without reducing future generations' ability to meet theirs.
Recycling and using waste materials are examples of sustainable production.

questions.question: Discuss the extent to which these companies are reducing the conflict between human needs, climate change and conservation, using the question, the photographs and own knowledge.
questions.answer: They reduce the conflict to some extent by cutting waste, landfill and burning and reducing oil-based fibres, but cotton and animal-based textiles still use land, water and chemicals.
steps: Recycling removes dyes and makes new fibres, reducing textile waste sent to landfill or burned.
Burning and landfill release greenhouse gases and pollution, so less waste lowers emissions.
Using wheat straw, wood waste and leather scraps reduces waste and the need for new land, crops and crude oil.
Making fibres from waste reduces the demand for crude oil (fossil fuel), lowering the climate impact of textiles.
Cotton farming, as shown in the photographs, still needs large areas of land, water and pesticides, so conflict with conservation remains.
The companies are a partial solution; their overall effect depends on their scale, energy use and whether total demand falls.

questions.question: Explain why a large spleen would help a seal during its dive, given that the spleen stores oxygenated red blood cells released during a dive.
questions.answer: A large spleen stores many oxygenated red blood cells, released into the blood during the dive, supplying extra oxygen for aerobic respiration without breathing.
steps: The spleen stores many red blood cells containing haemoglobin bound to oxygen.
During a dive these cells are released into the bloodstream, increasing the blood's oxygen-carrying capacity.
The extra oxygen is delivered to respiring muscles and organs, allowing aerobic respiration to continue.
So the seal can stay underwater longer, delaying the switch to anaerobic respiration and lactic acid build-up.

questions.question: Which term describes the middle value of a set of data? A mean, B median, C mode, D standard deviation.
questions.answer: B: median.
steps: The median is the middle value when the data are placed in order.
The mean is the average of all values, so it is not the middle value.
The mode is the most frequent value.
The standard deviation measures spread, so option B is correct.

questions.question: Describe two conclusions that can be made from the graph of spleen volumes of the Saluan and Bajau people.
questions.answer: The Bajau have larger spleens: their median volume (about 170 cm^3) is about 1.5 times that of the Saluan (about 110 cm^3), and their volumes are more variable (about 40 to 283 cm^3 against about 40 to 170 cm^3).
steps: The median spleen volume of the Bajau (about 170 cm^3) is higher than that of the Saluan (about 110 cm^3), so the Bajau have larger spleens on average.

The Bajau data are more spread out: the interquartile range is about 135 to 230 cm^3 (95 cm^3) against about 86 to 140 cm^3 (54 cm^3) for the Saluan, and the largest Bajau spleen is about 283 cm^3 against about 170 cm^3.
The two ranges overlap, with the same lowest value (about 40 cm^3), so some Bajau have spleens no larger than Saluan spleens.

questions.question: Explain how the Bajau could have become genetically adapted to diving, using the information in the question and own knowledge.
questions.answer: Random mutations affecting spleen size arose; divers with larger spleens survived and reproduced more, so the alleles became common over generations.
steps: Random mutations arise in the genome, some affecting genes that control spleen size.
Free-diving gives individuals with larger spleens an advantage, as they can dive longer and find more food.
Divers with these alleles survive and reproduce more successfully than others.
The beneficial alleles are inherited, so their frequency increases in the population over generations (natural selection).
The Bajau have dived for over 1000 years, which is enough time for this selection to shape the population.
The genome analysis found genetic differences linked to spleen volume, supporting a genetic cause.

questions.question: Suggest two reasons why very little of the light energy falling on a field of plants is absorbed and transferred to higher trophic levels.
questions.answer: Much light is reflected or transmitted through leaves, and light of some wavelengths is not absorbed by the pigments.
steps: Much light is reflected from leaf surfaces, especially green light that chlorophyll does not absorb.
Some light passes straight through the leaves (transmitted) without being absorbed.
Light falling on bare soil and non-photosynthetic parts is not absorbed by plant tissue.
Some absorbed light is lost as heat, and only a small fraction is converted into biomass.

questions.question: Only one fifteenth of the 1 700 000 kilocalories of light energy falling on one square metre in one year is converted into plant biomass. Calculate this energy in standard form.
questions.answer: 1.13 x 10^5 kilocalories.
steps: Divide the total by 15: 1 700 000 / 15.
Write in standard form to 3 significant figures: 1.13 x 10^5 kilocalories.
Check: 15 x 113 333 is about 1 700 000.

questions.question: Only 6 kilocalories became animal biomass. Calculate the number of kilojoules, given 1 kilocalorie = 4.2 kJ, to two significant figures.
questions.answer: 25 kJ.
steps: Multiply the energy in kilocalories by the conversion factor: 6 x 4.2.
Round to two significant figures: 25 kJ.
The unit is kJ, as asked.

questions.topic: Percentage Passed To Top Trophic Level
questions.question: In another field 154 000 kilocalories of energy was converted into plant biomass, and only 25 kilocalories was passed on to the highest trophic level. Calculate the percentage passed on.
steps: Divide the energy passed on by the energy in plant biomass: 25 / 154 000.
Multiply by 100 to give a percentage: 0.0162%.
Very little energy is passed up the food chain, showing low transfer efficiency.

questions.question: Which row of the table identifies the box representing NPP, the box representing GPP and the box representing respiration in the productivity diagram?
questions.answer: C: Box J is GPP, Box K is respiration (R) and Box L is NPP.
steps: Box J receives the input from photosynthesis, so it is gross primary productivity (GPP).
Part of the GPP is lost as respiration (box K) and the rest is net primary productivity (box L), since NPP = GPP - R.
The biomass distribution to leaves, wood and roots comes from box L, the NPP.

questions.question: Which are suitable units for NPP? A kJ m yr-1, B kJ m-1 yr-2, C kJ m-2 yr2, D kJ m-2 yr-1.
questions.answer: D: kJ m^-2 yr^-1.
steps: NPP is energy stored as biomass per unit area per unit time.
Energy is in kJ; area gives m^-2; time gives yr^-1.
Option A lacks the area exponent, B has m^-1 and yr^-2, and C has yr^2 instead of yr^-1.
So option D, kJ m^-2 yr^-1, is correct.

questions.question: A biomass of 12 500 a.u. is distributed 34% to leaves and 37% to roots, with the rest to wood. Calculate the biomass distributed to the wood.
steps: Wood receives the remainder: 100 - 34 - 37 = 29%.
Multiply: 12 500 x 0.29.
Check: leaves 4250 + roots 4625 + wood 3625 = 12 500.

questions.topic: Biomass Content Of Leaves And Roots
questions.question: Which row of the table shows what can be found in the biomass of the leaves and roots of trees?
questions.answer: C: leaves contain chlorophyll and starch, and roots contain starch and protein.
steps: Leaves have chloroplasts with chlorophyll and make and store starch.
Roots contain no chlorophyll, but store starch and contain protein (e.g. enzymes and membrane proteins).
Glycogen is an animal and fungal storage molecule and is not found in plants, so rows B and D are wrong; row A is wrong because roots have no chlorophyll.

questions.question: State what is meant by the term ecosystem, given that forests are examples of ecosystems.
questions.answer: A community of living organisms interacting with each other and with their abiotic (non-living) environment in an area.
steps: An ecosystem is a community of organisms in a defined area.
It includes biotic (living) and abiotic (non-living) components.
The organisms interact with each other and with the environment, e.g. through energy flow and nutrient cycles.
A forest is an example of an ecosystem.

questions.question: Which term describes the events that changed the extinct volcano into a habitat for many species? A entomology, B evolution, C speciation, D succession.
questions.answer: D: succession.
steps: Succession is the gradual change of bare ground into a community over time.
Here bare volcanic rock became a habitat for many species over thousands of years.
Entomology is the study of insects, so it is not relevant.
Evolution and speciation describe genetic change, not the development of a community.

questions.question: Which term describes the species of lizards found only on Redonda? A Archaea, B endemic, C epigenetic, D sustainable.
questions.answer: B: endemic.
steps: Endemic means found naturally in only one place.
The lizards occur only on Redonda, so they are endemic to the island.
Archaea are a domain of microorganisms, not a term for where a species lives.
Epigenetic and sustainable do not describe where a species is found.

questions.topic: How Rats And Goats Destroyed Wildlife
questions.question: Suggest how the rats and goats destroyed the wildlife on Redonda, using the photographs.
questions.answer: Goats graze plants and trample vegetation, while rats eat seeds, eggs and young lizards, removing food and habitat.
steps: Goats eat plants and trample vegetation, which removes food and shelter for native species.
Rats eat seeds, plants, eggs and young lizards, causing losses of prey and species.
Without vegetation, the soil erodes and the habitat becomes bare rock again.
Native species such as the endemic lizards cannot survive, so the wildlife was destroyed.

questions.question: Describe how to determine the biodiversity of Redonda to show the effectiveness of the conservation project.
questions.answer: Use random quadrats or transects to sample, count species and individuals, calculate a diversity index, and compare with earlier surveys over time.
steps: Use random sampling with quadrats or transects across different parts of the island.
Count the number of species and the number of individuals of each species in each sample.
Calculate a biodiversity index (e.g. Simpson's index) or species richness.
Repeat the survey over time and compare with data from before the 2016 project to show whether biodiversity has increased.

questions.question: State the meaning of the term succession.
questions.answer: The gradual change in the species composition of a community in an area over time, from pioneer species to a climax community.
steps: Succession is a sequence of changes in the community of an area over time.
It starts with pioneer species colonising bare ground.
Each stage changes the habitat, allowing new species to replace the earlier ones.
It ends in a stable climax community.

questions.question: Which of the following describes a habitat? A a group of interacting organisms, B a place that meets the environmental conditions an organism needs to survive, C the number of one species found in a particular place, D the niche of an organism.
questions.answer: B.
steps: A habitat is the place where an organism lives.
It must provide the environmental conditions the organism needs to survive.
A is a community, C is a population size, and D is a niche (role), not a place.
So B is the correct definition.

questions.question: Explain the changes in the numbers of alder, spruce and hemlock with time after the glacier has retreated, using the graph.
questions.answer: Alder, the pioneer, rises first and then disappears by 130 years; hemlock and spruce increase later and replace it, with spruce peaking at 110 years and then falling while hemlock stays at 18 per km^2, as in primary succession.
steps: Alder (pioneer) appears first (5 per km^2 at 20 years) and reaches 19 per km^2 at about 80 years; it fixes nitrogen, so adds nitrates and organic matter to the bare soil.
The improved soil allows hemlock (from 20 years, 18 per km^2 by 80 years) and spruce (rising to 20 per km^2 at 110 years) to establish.
Alder falls from about 80 years and reaches zero at 130 years because spruce and hemlock grow taller and shade it, so it loses the competition for light.

Spruce then falls from 20 to 9 per km^2 by 200 years, while hemlock remains steady at 18, because hemlock is better adapted to the shaded conditions and outcompetes spruce, giving a stable climax community.

questions.question: In 1863 there were 150 000 hares. Calculate how many times more hares there were than lynx.
steps: Read the graph for 1863: the number of lynx is about 22 x 10^3 = 22 000.
Number of times more hares = 150 000 / 22 000 = 6.8, so about 7.

questions.question: Sketch a line on graph 2 to show the likely changes in the numbers of hares from 1855 to 1880.
questions.answer: A cyclic line with the same 10-year cycle as the lynx, with each peak and trough about 1 to 2 years before the lynx peak and trough, and always above the lynx line.
steps: Draw a wavy line on graph 2 from 1855 to 1880 with peaks at about 1865 and 1875, about 1 to 2 years before the lynx peaks (about 1866 and 1876).
The hare minima should be at about 1860 and 1870, just before the lynx minima (about 1861 and 1871).
The hare line must be above the lynx line throughout, because hares are more numerous than lynx, and its peaks should be higher.

questions.question: Explain the changes in the numbers of lynx and hares.
questions.answer: When hares increase, lynx have more food and increase; more predation then reduces hares, so lynx later decline from lack of food, forming a cycle.
steps: When hare numbers rise, there is more food for lynx.
Lynx survive better and breed more, so lynx numbers increase after a short time lag.
Increased predation reduces the hare population.
With less food, lynx starve or breed less, so their numbers fall, letting hares recover and the cycle repeats.

questions.question: Suggest two reasons why the relationship between one predator species and one prey species is not always predictable.
questions.answer: Other predator and prey species, and environmental factors such as weather, disease and food availability, also affect both populations.
steps: Other predator species can also eat the prey, changing its numbers.
Other prey species may be eaten instead, so the predator's numbers do not follow one prey closely.
Weather, disease and seasonal food availability can change both populations independently of each other.
Alternative food sources and migration also break the simple link between one predator and one prey.

questions.question: Label the Tpiv for turtles on the graph (the temperature at which equal numbers of males and females are produced).
questions.answer: Tpiv is labelled on the x-axis at the temperature where the turtle curve passes through 50% males.
steps: Find the point halfway between 0 and 100% males (50%) on the y-axis.
Draw a horizontal line across to the turtle curve and a vertical line down to the temperature axis.
Label the point on the temperature axis where the line meets it as Tpiv.

questions.question: Describe the effect of the temperature of the sand on the percentage of males produced in these three reptiles.
questions.answer: Turtles: % males falls from 100% to 0% as sand temperature rises; tuatara: % males rises from 0% to about 100% as it rises; crocodiles: % males is high only in a middle range of temperature, and low at both low and high temperatures.
steps: Turtle: low temperatures give 100% males, and the percentage of males falls steeply over a narrow range (around the pivotal temperature) to 0% at high temperatures, so high temperature gives females.
Tuatara: the opposite, with about 0% males at low temperature rising to almost 100% males at high temperature.
Crocodile: males about 0% at low temperature, rising to nearly 100% at an intermediate range of temperatures, then falling to 0% again at high temperature, so females are produced at both extremes.

questions.question: Explain how temperature determines the sex of turtles, using the graph in part (a) and the diagram.
questions.answer: Temperature switches on one of two gene expression pathways: at lower temperatures the genes for DMRT1, Sox9 and AMH are expressed and the embryo develops male organs, whereas at higher temperatures CIRP and aromatase are expressed and it develops female organs.
steps: The graph shows that for turtles a low sand temperature gives about 100% males and a high temperature gives about 0% males, with a pivotal temperature between at which equal numbers are produced.
The diagram shows that temperature acts at the stage of development where the pathway divides, so it determines which genes are transcribed and translated.
At the male-producing temperatures the genes for the three proteins DMRT1, Sox9 and AMH are expressed, so the embryo develops male sex organs.
At the female-producing temperatures the genes for CIRP and aromatase are expressed instead, so female sex organs develop.

questions.question: Name one other anthropogenic activity that could affect the temperature of sand.
questions.answer: Burning fossil fuels (causing global warming), or urbanisation and construction such as deforestation.
steps: Anthropogenic activities change sand temperature directly or through climate change.
Burning fossil fuels releases greenhouse gases that warm the atmosphere and the sand.
Urbanisation and construction add heat-absorbing surfaces and remove shading vegetation.
Any one of these is an acceptable answer, e.g. burning fossil fuels.

questions.question: Discuss whether scientists should be concerned that microplastics could be endangering turtles, using all the information including the graph and table.
questions.answer: Yes, there is some cause for concern: sand with microplastic is warmer (30.294 and 30.473 C against 30.047 C), and as the control is already above the pivotal temperatures it would produce even more females, but the rise is small compared with the variation, so more evidence is needed.
steps: Microplastic raises the mean sand temperature by 0.25 C (25%) and 0.43 C (30%), and the graph shows the difference is positive on most days, so more microplastic gives more warming.

The control mean (30.047 C) is already above the pivotal temperatures for flatback (29.4 C) and green turtles (30.0 C), so mostly females are produced; microplastic increases the temperature further, towards the 31.1 C at which all are female (a 0.43 C rise is about 13% of the 3.4 C range from 27.7 to 31.1 C), so the sex ratio would be even more female-biased.
Too few males would reduce breeding success and genetic diversity, so populations could fall and turtles (already endangered) would be more at risk.

Against this: the standard deviations (about 3 C) are much larger than the differences (0.25 to 0.43 C), so the effect may not be significant; the tubs are small and short term, not natural beaches, and 25 to 30% microplastic is probably higher than on most beaches.
Conclusion: scientists should be concerned and should investigate natural beaches and use statistics, because even a small rise could change the sex ratio.

questions.question: Calculate the percentage increase in the total number of tigers in the world from 2010 (3200 tigers) to 2023 (5574 tigers).
steps: Increase = 5574 - 3200 = 2374 tigers.
Percentage increase = 2374 / 3200 x 100.
2374 / 3200 x 100 = 74.19%, which is 74.2% to one decimal place.
The tiger population grew by about three quarters over 13 years.

questions.question: Which is the ratio of Bengal tigers to other types of tigers in the world in 2023? A 0.556 : 1, B 0.798 : 1, C 1.253 : 1, D 1 : 1.798.
steps: Total tigers in 2023 = 5574; Bengal tigers = 3100.
Other tigers = 5574 - 3100 = 2474.
Ratio Bengal : other = 3100 / 2474 = 1.253, so 1.253 : 1.
Option C is correct.

questions.topic: Importance Of Proving Tigers In Bhutan
questions.question: Give two reasons why it was important to prove that tigers were present in Bhutan, especially in the mountain regions.
questions.answer: It shows that a population exists to be protected, and identifies where habitat and corridors are needed for the plan.
steps: Presence confirms that a population exists that can be protected and built upon.
It shows which mountain regions the tigers use, so habitat there can be protected.
It justifies funding and the plan to the government and conservation groups.
Records of presence show where a corridor linking tiger populations could be established.

questions.question: Deduce the importance of establishing a tiger corridor in Bhutan for a greater increase in the number and diversity of tigers, using the first map.
questions.answer: The corridor links isolated tiger populations, allowing movement and gene flow, which increases population size and genetic diversity.
steps: The map shows tiger populations in separate dark-shaded areas in India and neighbouring countries.
Bhutan lies between these populations, so a corridor through it would link them.
Linked populations can exchange individuals, giving gene flow and more alleles.
Greater genetic diversity and larger breeding populations reduce inbreeding and allow tigers to colonise new areas.
